# Sharing a local page over HTTPS

<!-- practices:learn:start (generated by scripts/practices/practices.py; do not edit) -->
**Learn this:** [Share over HTTPS](https://github.com/evocaslab/hq/blob/main/practices/explainers/share-over-https/index.html) (explainer). Learner path: Security, step 2.
<!-- practices:learn:end -->

For a page or tool on your machine that another device must open: a phone on the same WiFi, your laptop on another
network, a guest. Public sites (canonical host, HSTS) are in [web-https-hsts-and-redirects.md](https://github.com/evocaslab/hq/blob/main/practices/web-https-hsts-and-redirects.md);
the one-file page itself is in [wasm-self-contained-pages.md](wasm-self-contained-pages.md); diagrams in
[diagrams-as-code.md](diagrams-as-code.md). Checked 2026-11-07; what was not checked is listed at the end.

## Rules

1. **Ask first whether the page needs a server.** A one-file page (inline script, data and wasm) opens from `file://`,
   so send the file. HTTPS is needed only for APIs restricted to secure contexts: service workers and the Clipboard API
   (MDN), and anything that needs cross-origin isolation (`SharedArrayBuffer`; the page must send `COOP: same-origin` and
   `COEP`). WebAssembly itself is not the reason: our one-file wasm page works from `file://`.
2. **Reach comes before trust.** A certificate cannot make a private address reachable from another network. For
   "other network" use a private overlay (Tailscale) or a public tunnel; for "same WiFi" any route works.
3. **Change as little of the other device as you can.** Installing a root CA on a phone for one page is the most
   expensive route. Order: nothing to install (file, public tunnel), then a client the person already runs (Tailscale),
   then a trusted root last.
4. **There is no certificate "valid for any address".** Wildcards cover names (`*.lan.example`), never IPs. An IP needs
   its own `subjectAltName: IP:` entry; the CN is ignored by browsers. A private IP cannot get a publicly trusted
   certificate: a CA you install is the only trust root for it.
5. **An unconstrained CA on a device is a master key** for every site that device visits. If you run your own CA:
   - keep `ca.key` offline or on the one machine, never copy it (mkcert's README says the same of `rootCA-key.pem`); hand
     out only `ca.crt`;
   - put a **critical `nameConstraints`** on it (one domain, or one private IP range), `pathlen:0`, and a short life
     (days or weeks, not the 3600 days of a default root);
   - issue leaf certificates of days, not years, `serverAuth` only;
   - remove the root from the device when the sharing is over.
6. **Serve one file from its own directory**, bound to the interface that needs it (loopback for yourself; the LAN
   address for a phone; never `0.0.0.0` by habit). Never serve a home folder, a repo root or a directory with
   `.env`, keys or `.git`.
7. **Never expose an editing server.** A server that writes files (a diagram editor, a dev server with a file API)
   stays on loopback with a random token on every request and a check of the `Host` header (DNS rebinding), as in
   [diagrams-as-code.md](diagrams-as-code.md). To share, render a read-only page and serve that.
8. **A public URL is a publication.** A tunnel makes the page reachable by anyone with the link: treat the content as
   published, add a login or a one-time PIN, and stop it when done. Public certificates are also logged in
   Certificate Transparency, so a hostname you certify is public (Tailscale warns about machine names).
9. **Stop after sharing.** Foreground processes die with the terminal; for `tailscale serve --bg` run
   `tailscale serve reset`; for a tunnel stop `cloudflared`. A firewall rule opened for the phone is closed again.

## Which route when

| Who opens it | Page needs secure context | Route |
| --- | --- | --- |
| You, on this machine | any | `http://localhost` or `127.0.0.1` is already a secure context (MDN); no certificate |
| Anyone | no | send the one file; or `python -m http.server` bound to the LAN address for a minute (plain HTTP, no TLS) |
| Your phone or laptop, same WiFi | yes | **Tailscale Serve** if the device runs Tailscale; else an own CA limited to that address range |
| Your device, another network | yes | **Tailscale Serve** (the tailnet carries it, no port opened) |
| Your team's devices, many days | yes | a real domain: a name under your domain pointing to a private IP, certificate by **DNS-01** (works for servers not reachable from the internet), Caddy or `certbot` renews |
| A guest, nothing to install | yes | a public tunnel (`cloudflared` quick tunnel, Tailscale Funnel, ngrok-style) with a login; or publish the static file |
| A guest, page is private | any | do not use a tunnel; send the file or a PDF |

## Routes in detail

### Tailscale Serve (first choice for your own devices)

- `tailscale serve --bg 3000` shares a local server inside the tailnet over HTTPS; a file or directory needs root
  (`sudo tailscale serve /path/index.html`); `tailscale serve status` shows it, `tailscale serve reset` clears all.
  Funnel (`tailscale funnel`) is the public variant, ports 443, 8443, 10000 only.
- The certificate is a Let's Encrypt one for the machine's `*.ts.net` name, so every device trusts it with no install.
  It requires MagicDNS and "Enable HTTPS" in the admin console, and the machine name goes to the public CT log.
- Every device that opens the page runs the Tailscale client and is in the tailnet; this is also the limit (a guest is not).

### Own CA (same network, devices you control)

Why not a self-signed leaf: each browser shows a warning and some APIs stay blocked; a CA you trust once signs many leaves.

```bash
# CA: constrained, short-lived, offline key (a CA file, not a leaf)
openssl req -x509 -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -noenc -days 30 -config ca.cnf -keyout ca.key -out ca.crt
# leaf for one IP (openssl.cnf has extensions in leaf.ext: CA:FALSE, serverAuth)
openssl req -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -noenc -subj "/CN=leaf" -addext "subjectAltName=IP:192.168.1.20" -keyout leaf.key -out leaf.csr
openssl x509 -req -in leaf.csr -copy_extensions copy -extfile leaf.ext -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial -days 7 -out leaf.crt
```

`ca.cnf` section: `basicConstraints=critical,CA:TRUE,pathlen:0`, `keyUsage=critical,keyCertSign,cRLSign`,
`nameConstraints=critical,permitted;IP:192.168.0.0/255.255.0.0,permitted;DNS:lan.test`. Tried locally with OpenSSL 3.5.5:
a leaf for `192.168.1.20` verifies (`-verify_ip`), a leaf for `10.0.0.5` from the same CA fails with
"permitted subtree violation", and the wrong IP fails with "IP address mismatch". **Whether each browser enforces
IP constraints on a user-installed root is not verified here**; test with a browser, or the BetterTLS suite, before relying on it.
- **mkcert** does the same without the constraint: `mkcert -install` (local CA into system, NSS/Firefox and Java stores),
  `mkcert 192.168.1.20 localhost` (IPs are plain arguments), `mkcert -CAROOT` shows where `rootCA.pem` and its key live;
  for another device copy `rootCA.pem` only. It is a development tool, not for other people's machines.
- **Caddy** has an internal CA: a site block with `tls internal` (root 3600 days, intermediate 7 days, leaf 12 h by default);
  it installs the root on the same machine, and `caddy trust` / `caddy untrust` add or remove it. Whether it issues for a
  bare IP address was not found in the docs. `caddy file-server --root <dir> --listen :8443` serves a directory but the
  flags alone give TLS only with `--domain` on a public name, so use a Caddyfile for a LAN address.
- **miniserve**: `miniserve --tls-cert leaf.crt --tls-key leaf.key -p 8443 -i 192.168.1.20 file.html`; without `-i` it binds
  all interfaces, so always pass `-i`. Whether TLS needs a build feature was not found in the README.

Install the root only on devices you own:

| Device | Steps (source) |
| --- | --- |
| Debian/Ubuntu | copy PEM as `/usr/local/share/ca-certificates/<name>.crt`, `sudo update-ca-certificates` (Debian man page). Firefox and Chrome do not read it automatically |
| Firefox (any OS) | own store; set policy `ImportEnterpriseRoots` or `security.enterprise_roots.enabled` to use the OS store (Windows, macOS), or the `Install` policy with a file in the Mozilla certificates folder (Mozilla wiki) |
| Windows | `certutil -addstore` / `-user` exist (Microsoft docs); the store name `Root` is from memory |
| macOS | Keychain Access then set "Always Trust"; or `sudo security add-trusted-cert -d -r trustRoot -k /Library/Keychains/System.keychain ca.crt` (seen in vendor scripts; not checked against Apple's man page) |
| iOS | open the file to install the profile, then Settings, General, About, Certificate Trust Settings, turn on full trust (Apple) |
| Android | Settings, Security and privacy, More security settings, Encryption and credentials, install a certificate (Google Pixel help). Apps and some browsers may ignore user roots (mkcert README) |
| Chrome on Linux | uses the NSS database `~/.pki/nssdb`; a `certutil -d sql:` command is the usual way (not verified) |

### A real domain (for a team, a lab)

A name you own (`dev.example.com`) with an A record to a private IP is legal. A public CA cannot validate it by HTTP,
but **DNS-01** works for servers not reachable from the internet and for wildcards (Let's Encrypt); it needs DNS API
credentials on the host, so use a narrow token. Names go to the CT log. Public certificate lifetimes are shrinking
(CA/Browser Forum SC-081v3: 200 days from 2026-03-15, 100 days from 2027-03-15, 47 days from 2029-03-15), so automate
renewal; this limit applies to public CAs only, not to your own root. Let's Encrypt also issues IP-address
certificates (profile `shortlived`, 160 hours); I did not verify how an IP is validated, but a private IP cannot be
proven from the internet, so this is not a LAN route (inference).

### Public tunnel

`cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:8080` gives a random `trycloudflare.com` URL until stopped; no account needed;
no uptime guarantee, 200 in-flight requests, no SSE, the name changes each time; `--allowed-mail` adds a one-time PIN
(Cloudflare docs). ngrok-style services work the same way and were not checked.

## Lessons (from building `hq-diagram` sharing, 2026-11-07)

- **The best share was no server**: the rendered page is one file; HTTPS was asked for before anyone checked which API needed it.
- **Reach and trust are two problems.** A cert for a private IP fixed nothing for a device on another network.
- **Bind and path are the blast radius.** The same command is safe on `127.0.0.1` with one file and unsafe on `0.0.0.0` with a repo root.
- **Recipe, not recollection**: put the sequence (render, serve one file, optional `tailscale serve`, print the URL, stop) in one
  command so nobody re-derives the flags; see [prepared-commands.md](prepared-commands.md).
- Chrome's Local Network Access prompt (Chrome 142, since 2025-09) covers public pages calling private addresses, not a page served from a LAN host
  (first milestone); a hosted page that fetches your LAN tool will be asked about.

## Not verified

Browser enforcement of IP `nameConstraints` on user roots (Chrome, Safari, Firefox); Windows store name; macOS `security`
flags; Chrome NSS commands; whether `tls internal` covers a bare IP; whether miniserve TLS needs a feature; ngrok;
Android app behaviour; `python -m http.server` flags (from memory); that wasm needs no secure context (the MDN list of restricted features was not read; our own
`file://` run says it works).
